My 2 cents about touch trades are as follows. 1. you need a solid trend in place on the chart your trading, don't really care what the tf is 2. you need to watch out for areas that might cause it to stall, so if price stalled out earlier in the day at an area around where you are taking a touch trade be careful. 3. G'day peoples! Here is the first version of my modified MA. I use all the colors the same for each MA and only change the line thickness to show trending v flat. This is all that is required and I don't want to "busy up" the charts with psychedelic indicator patterns! You can change colors for "up" and "down" etc, but I advise against it. (Personal preference). The "Trend_Minimum" parameter changes the line attributes when the slope of the line exceeds this many pips per bar. This is far better than playing with angles, as angles vary with the price scale. For example, if you are in a period where the price is ranging your chart may only be 50 pips high, if then there is a breakout for 100 pips or so, your chart is now 150 pips high - that's three times bigger! What would have been a 45 degree trendline now would be only 26 degrees! So angles are very deceptive, whether expressed as degrees or "clock hours". One thing I always do so that my charts are consistent it to select "scale fix" in chart properties and adjust the scale to 10 pips per price marker on the side. Then, 10 pips always LOOKS like 10 pips, etc! There's enough to confuse the trader without rubbery charts adding to it! I have found the best values for the 10 EMA to be about 1.5 and the others about 0.8.... but you are best to play around with it yourself. Now the problem of when is a "touch" a "touch" and when is it not a "touch"! Remember that the MAs are all based on the "Close", and since the current candle has not yet closed, that wiggling line is NOT the "10EMA" and is actually meaningless! See what Clay had to say.... http://www.forexfactory.com/showpost...&amp;postcount=671 So, it takes a bit of discretion here, folks, and maybe price action on lower time frames will aid you to speculate where the "touch" is! Now, in this version, the first thing that MAY help is that you can turn off the "Serpent's tongue". Setting "Show_tongue" to false will simply show a horizontal line for the current candle. Next, I will be adding a three other stable lines that will maybe help.... All this is experimental, and if it help, good, if not then "back to the drawing board"! I've attached a few images what my chart looks like and settings for the 10 EMA. ..... and I noticed on those images that I've missed an opportunity while messing with this, so, just Google "Bigtent's bank account" and donate half your profits from this period to compensate me. Conforming with my boundless generosity, I'll let you keep your losses (I have enough of my own).

--- 帖子 #3462 ---
With a higher stop loss, you can preserve your account by reducing your lot size. This means you won't make as much per pip. But if you trade a higher time frame, you might make up the difference by getting bigger gains. You can determine lot size as follows. Figure out what percentage you are willing to lose in a horrible day. By dance rules, a horrible day means two consecutive losses and you are out. Lets say that you are willing to take an x% hit for the day. Thus on each trade, you are willing to lose up to x/2% for the day. So the dollar amount you are willing to lose is your starting Equity for the day times x/200. Next, figure the pip value for the currency. (With USD denominated pairs, its $10/pip for standard lots, $1/pip for minis). For other pairs it gets more complicated and probably easier to use an online pip calculator, or maybe an EA. Finally, figure out your maximum stop loss for the time frame you are using. In the dance, the rule is 19 pips. It will be different for higher time frames, and it might be different if you focus on a particular type of trade, like constrainments. The formula for lot size then is: (Equity*x/200) / (Pip Value)*(MaxStopLoss) For an example for basic dance trading. Suppose you had a starting Equity of $10,000, were willing to risk 5% over two losses in a day, were trading GBPUSD, and using the dance maximum stop loss of 19. Thus, your lot size would be (10,000 * 5/ 200) / (10 * 19) = (250)/(190) = 1.31 standard lots. Even with bigger stop losses, you can use the same kind of technique to trade with larger stop losses without necessarily risking your account. The question is not the absolute size of the stop loss, but how often the trades win and how much they return when they do win.

It is simple if you make it simple. Just learn the method, focus on the best opportunities and get rid of your fears &amp; greed. Dance is just one of several trading strategies that are profitable if you just follow the basic rules. The problem is that usually we overcomplicate things and then trading becomes difficult. For me, Dance opened my eyes and helped me see the market flowing with the help of the MAs, RNs, etc. But I was experienced with trading already. So if you are new to trading you will have to pay your tuition fees one way or the other. Sticking to this strategy will help you minimize the fees and start becoming profitable. My advice if you choose to stay around is to trade exclusively the Dance in DEMO for 2-3 months and if you get positive, open a small account to trade with real money (even pennies, just REAL). Only if you graduate these two steps you can start with a regular account. Kostas

--- 帖子 #3513 ---
Yes, you are right. I know I'm not catching the touch, but that is always a problem on the 10 EMA. In the manual, many of the examples of 10 EMA touches show a bar where the wick just touches the MA. In real time, when that bar was at the "touch price", it was not touching the EMA line. There would be a lot fewer signals if you waited for price to actually hit the wiggling line. It is a moving average of the close, and that means you can't tell where the MA is going to be until the close of the candle. That's why I call that line "the serpent's tongue" - it is very deceptive and unreliable. Clay talked about this in the Dance thread here , and it requires some discretion. I have been trying to work this out using price action on the M5/M1, but I haven't nailed it yet, as it is not quite the same as that of higher time frames. For example, I should have waited for Cable to go lower, as I was actually expecting it to do so, but I misread the M1 price action and jumped the gun. The Aussie was difficult as the two losses were "shooting" for the 10 EMA on the first two bars. The trade that I finally got was after the third bar and on the H1 10 EMA and the M15 50. I still missed this by 5 pips or so, as it shot down and bounced back so quick, it was impossible to catch it "at the touch". By the time I clicked and the order was placed, it was back up at the top of that long tailed doji on the M5. The only way to learn this stuff is in real time, as you can't do it in the simulator because you only have one time frame (although I'm looking for some ways around that - such as Stratman's minicharts as used in the THV system). As for the stop losses on the two losers, they were 10 and 11 pips, which is about what Clay recommends, in fact he often suggests SMALLER ones in these cases, and says that if you are needing larger stops, then your entries are the problem, and this is what I am working on. In fact, If I'd had smaller stops, then I would have perhaps fared better, as I would not have had so much to recoup before I went into profit. I'm only using a penny a pip account, so I don't need to fret, and I'll get it right..... eventually, LOL! Hey, it's pretty good when you can make blunders (i.e. learn lessons) like this and still end up positive for the session! Profitable education!

--- 帖子 #3517 ---
I think you misunderstood what I was talking about there. It's not a case of "demanding" anything, the system being BS or anyone being an idiot. "Recoup" is just a term and it is a fact of trading that you will get losses, and you will recoup those with profitable trades. It's not to be confused with "revenge trading", etc. It's simple arithmetic and it occurs whether you think about it or not. If you take the inevitable losses, then you must "recoup" that loss before you make actually are in profit. I lost about 2% on the first two trades, but the next two I made around 3% profit, giving me around 1% profit overall. So I "recouped" the 2% loss. But you are very right about psychology. My target was 3%, but I was only able to make 1% as I'd made poor entries. I will always keep a track of where I am up to, but that doesn't mean that I'm going to get into "revenge trading" or the like. It also doesn't mean that I will let the losses stop me (fear) from making a better entry and making a profit. I was happy with the positive result, even though I hadn't reached my target, I'd learned something (at least I hope I did)!

WOW! What a day for dancing!! If I ever needed proof that this is a phenomenal system, today was the day. Here are the trades I entered today for a total of +223 points. I honestly can't believe it. I wait until there is a big move and then take the first retrace. I used to try and catch a move as soon as it starts because I was afraid I'd miss it, and was always getting it wrong which was killing my balance and my confidence. I was always getting stopped out before by price just coming up and touching my SL, or I was freaking out when price went into the negative and closing the trade. Now I leave the SL and -10 and trust that I made the right entry. Those two things have made a huge difference to me and my results.

--- 帖子 #3536 ---
ok, here it goes, simple Elliot Wave theory for the Dancer http://www.forexfactory.com/attachme...1&amp;d=1295359469 Q. What are them waves thigie? A. Elliot Waves theory pretty much is about price unfolding and following the extremes in investor psychology. To simplify things lets say that that in a generally uptrending market the move will occur in 5 waves. 1, 3, 5 are up moves, 2 and 4 are down (corrective moves) and these are the ones we can use as "Touch Trades" as Dancers. The 1st wave is a warning that something is about to happen. The 2nd wave is a correction (retrace) but it never goes lower than the start of the 1st wave. The 3rd wave is the one you are looking for it is the largest of all 5. You should enter that at either the end of wave 2 or as soon as the price goes higher the high of wave 1. The 4th wave is a retrace, again it must not go below the high of wave 1. i usually dont enter those Unless there is a very good reason (ie no resistance above) The 5th wave is smaller than the 3rd,and sometimes its choppy or it doesnt even happen at all, if you are in it and you see the price hesitate you know its about time to tighten your stops. IF wave 2 breaks below the start of wave 1 then things are simple, the move has ended before it even started and you cant expect whatever follows to be along the lines above. IF wave 4 breaks below the high of wave 1 then the move is over and you better pull out asap. Q. How it relates to the dance? A. The pullbacks are good points for dance's "touch trades", expecting that they will happen doesnt make you feel like a fool that you missed the start of the move but rather comfort you that there will be more chances. -------------------------------------------------------------------- After the series of waves have ended you can expect a fall of the price, this time in 3 waves. A,B,C. Q. When is the best time to enter? A. After the A wave start going down you bang your head with the mouse because you missed the move, usually its a big one (could come after a constrainment of sorts) and you cant bellliiiieve you didnt see it. Great, so what do you do? you wait for a wave B. A retrace of the price usually to the 10EMA. I remember "Survivor" (or else Mr Constrainment) here in this thread saying that he doesnt any more feel bad because he missed the move because there will be a pullback so he can enter safely. --------------------------------------- you can expect the opposites of 12345 and ABC when trending Down. --------------------------------------- Keep in mind that the waves will not allways hold true but at least you know what to expect if you see one that is behaving nicely. --------------------------------------- I hope i didnt confuse you and isnt meant to be an addition to the method, but i feel it will help people be more patient and dont feel like they missed the trade. Also it will help those that have a special ability to nail the tops and bottoms of the very end of a move, believe me i was an expert in that too... now with our experience from the Dance we can expect certain areas to play the role of enpoints of these waves, because say a confluence is there, or a touch of the 10EMA on a retrace or a bounce off the 35/50 , a confluence of a RN and a MA , or pivot points with something of the above. Will they always hold true? Of course not, but at least you know what to expect, and if you see they dont behave as you would expect at that point just wait for the next. and an example of a very typical move below. http://www.forexfactory.com/attachme...1&amp;d=1295360135

--- 帖子 #3545 ---
Your sample chart is a very good illustration of Elliott Wave Theory, and also illustrates why I can't follow it. You have drawn a nice set of waves numbered 1-5 alongside the chart, and they sort of make sense after the fact. In real time however, I would see the first move up as coming from the low. That means the area you mark as 1, I would have considered the 3rd segment of the wave, and so on. Also, when price was above the top that you draw, I would probably still have thought that we were in segment 5. Except that I wouldn't have thought that, because my segment 5 would already have ended back at the top of the segment you call 3. Is this confusing enough yet? That's why I prefer the Dance. By the way, even after the fact, it looks to me like that trend has five impulses and four pull-backs. To make it fit the Elliott Wave, you really do have to ignore the first part of the move, and also the final, exhaustion area where the highs actually get hit. EDIT: By the way, I think you did a great job summarizing EW theory, and I understand why you did it. It's just an idea that I can't get my head around. In it's simple form, it seems very detail. But when I start looking at it in any detail, I realize that I'd have a better chance of becoming an international master at chess than actually making any money with EW.

Natnimrey, i am certainly not in right mood to do proper analysis. A killed day with -30 and a long vacation from tomorrow make it difficult for me to concentrate. Add to that some beer that i had But It's not a constrainment to me. Its more of a ping pong between 35/50. You enver know which way it will go. Remeber contrainment have only one MA constraining the price. when you see two MAs holding the price there is trouble. This is often a reason of losses with constrainment. For example, you see 35 holding it up but you don't see 10 holding it down. In your example price is being held by both 35 and 50. You never know who will win. Maybe HTF analysis may help. When you see such areas you may scalp it for what they are worth- Sell at top and buy back at low. and continue till it breaks out and hits your SL. But make sure its wide enough to give some room for scalp. And also you are just hoping that it wont breakout before you have scalped enough to be profitable after breakout hits your SL. Finally remeber that manual says this ping pong area business is only for experienced guys and if you havent mastered basic trades yet you should leave these trades alone as per manual. Hope that helps.

In all, there are five bars that reach or just barely reach the 50 on the upside, and one that blows through it to come back. I have a few questions for Survivor about milking constrainments. On the average, how many times would you say that you get to go back to the cow? (I mean, what percentage do you get 1 trip, what percentage 2, what percentage 3, and so on...) What would you say the typical take profit is for a successful constrainment? (This is just for the final move, not for any of the milking sessions) What percentage of the time do you get a winner on the final move, as opposed to ultimately going for a stop? The reason I'm asking is because I've set up a spreadsheet that allows me to compare a few different ways to approach the milking process, and those seem to be the key variables. I talked before about pyramiding your positions as opposed to simply taking your profits. Basically the more rounds to the dairy, the more pips gained on a winner, and the higher the winning percentage, the better it is to pyramid. Conversely, fewer trips to the dairy, lower take profit, and lower winning percentage all weigh in favor of taking your pips. I'd like to have some idea of what the actual numbers are. EDIT: Here are a couple of examples. They all use these same assumptions. Stop of 8. TP on milking rounds 16. One round of milking happens 1/2 the time. 2 rounds, 40%. 3+ rounds 10%. (These figures round up, but otherwise do not take into account trades where there were 4 or more rounds.) With 30 Take profit on the constrainment, and a 50% winning percentage, milking and pyramiding are almost dead even. With 30 Take profit and a 65% winning percentage, pyramiding wins by over 4 pips/trade. With 40 TP and 50% wins, pyramiding wins by over 7 pips/trade. With 40 TP and 65% wins, pyramiding wins by over 11 pips/trade With 50 TP and 50% wins, pyramiding wins by over 12 pips/trade With 50 TP and 65% wins, pyramiding wins by over 19 pips/trade From what you've been saying, I assume your success on Constrainments is well over 50%. But even at 50%, for milking to do better than pyramiding, you would either need a TP of less than 30 pips, or you there would have to be greater than 50% of the time that you only get to go to the dairy once. The figures would change some with differences in stop loss, and in the amount of pips milked each round. Finally, here is the upside example. Suppose you had a good constrainment that went for four full rounds before taking off for a 60 pip profit. With the milking method, you would end up with 140 pips. And you would rightfully be ecstatic: that's a weeks profit in one trade. But if you pyramided the same trade, you would end up with 436 pips -- and that's an entire month in one trade. Keep in mind, after the first round, they are both risk free trades. This is not an instance where greed leads to losers. The more conservative (and probably more consistent) approach is to milk your pips. But pyramiding here is free, and it looks to me like it is almost guaranteed to make you more in the long run.

The defaults of the scripts are 2% and 15 pip stop, which you can change to suit. The money management calculates the lot size so that if the stop is hit, only the specified percentage of your account will be lost. As your account grows the lot size grows, if you sustain losses it will reduce. They also open two positions, one with a take profit (based on the riskratio parameter - default is 1 which is the same as the stop) and the other has no target, so you can trail it as per the Dance rules or some other method. TRY ON DEMO FIRST!!!

Here you could take 15 pips on the second bar, or hold while it bounces for four more bars to squeeze out a few more pips. If you waited for it to hit one of the earlier support levels, you would break even. 4) 35 Bounce. Break Even. The 35 and 50 are far apart and diverging, but they are so steep that I’m not sure whether that matters. At the touch they are 26 pips apart, but the 35 is 77 degrees. If you took this on the first touch and moved to breakeven at 10, you would get taken out at breakeven. And I don’t think, in real time, that I would enter on the second test of this MA. 5) 50 Bounce. Winner. The 50 is really steep, and the 35 is now coming back up to meet it. This is a very odd picture. The touch off the 50 turns out to give a strong rejection. The only question is where and how to exit. In hindsight, the RN looks like a great place, but I have no idea first whether I really would have entered this trade, and second, how I would have exited with price moving that erratically. 6) Constrainment. Just outside the circle, there’s a near second touch of the 50, then seven more before the move finally occurs. With Survivor’s approach, I think it might be possible to play this for three 10 pip trips to the dairy before the trade finally moved. Final move, with a trailing stop was good for 30 pips. The trouble with this, however, is knowing that 10 pips was the right area to take your profits on the milk runs. 7) 50 Bounce. The MAs are starting to flatten and are parallel. It’s the dead time of the trading day. And this is like the 10th test or near test of the 50. (The 3rd test of an MA invalidates almost any trade. But what about the 10th? If the support has proven itself that well, does the trade become valid again?) All those things should mean that it’s a no trade. But it turns out it was still good for a scalp. Getting out at the RN would get 15 pips. As always, I would appreciate any comments/criticisms. I'm especially interested in the question of whether repeated respect for an MA makes a later bounce valid, where otherwise it would simply be a third touch and no trade. (Actually, I guess I'm asking whether a successful constrainment resets the touch count.)

--- 帖子 #3703 ---
Good point asos. Here is how I deal with confluence: 1. When I take signals from M15 then the points of interest should be within 4-5 pips. You probably have noticed in my posts when I repeat that price likes to touch all points of interest if they are close together. So, assume I have a RN and then 4-5 pips away the SMA 35 and another 4-5pips away the EMA 50. I wait using M1 to see the price touching all of them and then I get in. This is absolutely confluence. 2. When I take signals from H1, H4 then I am even more generous with confluence. I can wait 15 or 20pips for the price to check the points of interest and then I get in. Today EU was a good example. The price rushed through the MAs, then EMA62/Daily S1 were within a pip, and then through the RN 13 pips lower. I got in exactly on the RN at 8:17GMT with 15p SL. My target was just below daily pivot. P.S. FxPro sucked today. I lost service at GMT 9:58 and came back almost 2hrs later!!! I actually had a small trade (0.3lots) running short from Daily Pivot which hit the SL when I couldn't log on..... One more scare like that and I will move to FinFX.

--- 帖子 #3706 ---
I’m doing this exercise on a daily basis mostly to help build my confidence, and also in the hope that it will help me to spot these trades in real time. One of the surprising things that I’ve discovered in the last few days is how many opportunities appear, and also, how few of the decent opportunities turn out badly. 1) 35 Bounce. Winner. This is a bad trade. The MA’s are dead flat. It’s not quite yet to either the Frankfurt or London open. Even so, it would have been good for 25 pips with no drawdown. 2) 35 Bounce. Loser. Another bad trade. If anything, this one is worse than the last one, since the MAs are now diverging, and its now a second touch of the 35. (I’m noting these trades here mostly because these are exactly the kinds of trades that I seem to take and end up either losing or breaking even on. I’m pointing them out partially in an effort to cure me from taking them.) 3) 50 Bounce. Loser. This may be as bad as the last trade. It’s now a first touch. But it’s also going against the higher time frame directions, which are all bullish. 4) 35/50 Bounce. Winner. This is the first good trade, and probably the trade of the day. The 10 EMA has really steepened, and this could also be a 10 touch trade. The 35 and 50 now have converged and have some steepness to them. Also, there is almost perfect confluence of the S1. (There was a similar, first retrace to the 50 three bars earlier, but it didn’t make it to the 10 or the 35, so it was probably a missed trade, and I didn’t include it here.) This is another day in a row (I think this is four) where, after price crossed both the 35 and 50, the first retracement trade was worth big pips -- here 60+ with zero drawdown. 5) 10EMA Touch. Winner or Break Even. This is another example of a first touch of the 10 being good for a few pips after a big move, even when the retrace back to the 10 was a bit of a struggle. Here, price stalled out for 5 bars before the 10 finally caught up with it. And even then, it was still good for 13+ pips, if you got out early. Otherwise, it was a BE trade. 6) 10 EMA Touch. The 10 got steep enough again on what amounts to a new move. The retrace is two bars but didn’t quite make it to the 10. This is probably a trade that I would miss, even though it appears that these near touches are generally a decent bet. This one is worth 20-25 pips. If you waited three bars for the first real touch of the 10, you would probably either skip it because this wasn’t a big move, and price has stalled for 5 bars again. Or you would get a break even trade, if you were lucky. 7) 35 Bounce. Winner. The 35 is in confluence with the pivot and also with a strong S/R line. Without the confluence, I would think this trade should be passed on, mostly because of the width between the 35 and the 50. As it turns out, after moving 7 pips against the trade, and a wait of almost an hour, price shot up out of nowhere, and this would be good for about 30 pips at the RN above. I have a hard time, however, believing that I would take this trade. 8) 50 Bounce. Winner. This is another trade that I think I would have a hard time taking. After shooting up 35 pips like a rocket, price drops just faster to hit the 50. Here’s what Clay might say about this trade in the manual. You should watch the price come down to the 50 and then blow through it. When price then starts moving back up from the RN, you would keep watching. The close is almost exactly at the 50, moving up, and this is where he would say to enter, at the open of the new bar. (There are at least two examples of this kind of trade, either in the manual itself or in the Dance thread. I don’t know if I could do it, though it obviously turned into a really good trade.) By the way, even if you took this one as a touch trade on the way down, it still would have been a by the rules trade, and worth lots of pips, but with a medium scary 8 pip drawdown. 9) 10 EMA Touch, Winner. Another example of a first touch that doesn’t strictly follow the rules, but comes after a pretty big move. Here there are 5 full bars to get to the touch. I don’t think I could take this trade for exactly that reason. But it turns out to be worth 20+ pips after a full bar of drawdown of just over 8 pips. 10) 35 Touch. Winner. This one is late in the day and should probably be passed. I don’t know whether you count this as a first touch of the 35 or a fourth touch. The main thing this trade has in its favor is the confluence of the 35 with a RN. That combined with the steepness, and the overall trends of the higher time frames, may make this a worthwhile trade, despite the time of day, and despite the distance between the 35 and the 50. Overall, I guess this is an OK trade, but I would be on the fence about it, and probably pass it. (As a general rule of thumb, if its an iffy trade, and it became a winner, that means I would have passed on it. Conversely, iffy trades that lose are the ones that I jump on in a flash.) So look at that overall. If you just traded this mechanically for the full day, you would end up with 6-7 winners, 2 losers, and one or two break even trades. That’s pretty amazing stuff. I’m going to try to catch up with today’s chart later on.

This was a perfect illustration of how higher time frames prevail over short ones. If you traded this day with an eye to the H1 charts, you would do quite well and spare yourself much confusion and heartache. 1) This rectangle is a total mess. The 35 and 50 are flat and wobbly. The first touch of the 50, going with the prevailing uptrend, breaks even. If you took the touch after that (and I don't know what the reason would be for taking it), you would do pretty well. After that, everything is either a loser or a pure guess. But take a look at what's going on at the 100. (My black line) This same area makes perfect sense on the one hour chart. 2) 10 Touch. Winner. This is the first touch after a strong move. It hits right at an S/R line. The 10 is very steep, and its a very good trade, worth 20-40 pips, with a 4 pip drawdown. 3) 35/50 Bounce. Loser. To me this looks like an almost perfect bounce trade. The MAs are both steep. Maybe they have started diverging a little, but if this is enough to disqualify the trade, then a real bounce entry would be very rare indeed. It would have been better if there had been some real confluence with something else. Anyway, its a good trade and a loser. These things happen. 4) 10 EMA Touch. Winner or BE. This is only an OK trade. The 10 is steep, but the trade is counter the higher time frames. Also, there still has not been a retrace to the 35 or 50 since they crossed, so there's a decent possibility that the price would blow through here and test the 50 or 35. If you took this trade, you would have to either get out with 10 pips, or you would probably break even. (The first touches of the 35 and 50 after this are not trades because the MAs are flat, wide and diverging). 5) 10 Touch. Winner. 10 is steep. The 35 and 50 are right above it, within 9 pips. Trade is good for 15 pips at the RN, and up to 30 after that. Now for the H1 chart, and look how pretty it is compared to the M15. 6) The rectangular mess noted in (1) above turns out to be a constrainment on the 50 and 62 in the H1. I probably wouldn't have caught this one, but I think Survivor might have salivated over it. 7) The first touch of the 10 on the H1 after the big move. It ends up being good for 25+ pips, with zero drawdown. 8) Retest of the 50, 62, and 35 MAs, with a nearly perfect RN confluence. Even at the worst entrance, this would have a drawdown of only 11 pips, and is good for 25-30. (EDIT: This is the arrow on the second chart that doesn't have a number. Conclusion for the day is that when things are not making sense at the M15 level, take a look at the bigger picture.

I have tried to make an alert for the usage of Dance/CHOROS for fun. This indicator can allow user to set an alert so that if the close price of a bar is getting near (15 pips away for example) the EMA50 line (or other EMA parameter value), the MT4 will give an alert, and the user don't need to keep watching the chart of the pair when the price is hundred pip away from the EMA50. There is no gurantee the indicator works as expected, try at your own risk. The attached image shows where the alerts may have given when the indicator is turning on.

--- 帖子 #3746 ---
Not there yet. When I have time I added this to the indicator. At the moment, the parameter and the default value that you can use are: Gapping: how far away the bar close from the target line that you want the indicator to give you alert. The default value is 150 or 15 pip FasterEMA: 1 for using bar close as the checking value SlowerEMA: the moving average parameter you want to use as the target line. Default value is 50 and you may change it. SoundON: Once the bar close reach the attention region and give you an alert. You may turn it off, since no more alert is needed. TIPS: It is not necessary to add this indicator to the chart you usually watch and trade with. If you trade GBPUSD on a M15 chart, you can open another GBPUSD M15 chart and add the indicator to it and minimize it.

This is especially true since it is counter the higher time frames, and since the bottom bounce off a Round Number, an S/R line, and the Weekly R2. If anything, this is a good spot to be looking for a reversal. So it’s a loser but it should be a no trade.

As usual some very intelligent questions from duffy. Am still in vacation hangover but have just finished through the thread and it's time to answer. Sorry for delay. Hope you were aware that i was away without internet access. 1. "On the average, how many times would you say that you get to go back to the cow?" It's an infinite loop. Dont try to guess it just keep milking. When breakout happens you will always have one position open for big move so why worry. Sometimes i would milk it for 3 times sometimes 10 times. Doesn't matter to me. All i want is a clear entry point and Sl as long as price keeps coming back to my entry points i will keep milking. But average is tough to guess. Experience helps here. I find Fast movers like EU and GU rarely giving more than 2 milkings before blow. But slow movers like CAd and CHF keep at one constrainment for whole Europe sessions and breakout at only NY sessions. So maybe 6-7 milkings. Again it's experimental observation. 2. "What would you say the typical take profit is for a successful constrainment?" That's tough one as dance doesn't tell when to take profit. What i do is i trail as per original manual (SL moves to low of previous 15M candle after every 15M close). That's because i find constrainments to be monster movers and don't want to miss entire action. However, if i find a confluence of resistance / support against my trade and am happy with my pip count -say 50 and above- i get out. On an average i would say 70 pips for fast movers and 40 fr slow ones should be good tp levels (for constrainments in 1H) 3. "What percentage of the time do you get a winner on the final move, as opposed to ultimately going for a stop?" It's exceptionally high. I used to get almost 8090% at last count but now i have stopped counting. Good constrainments NEVER fail in my opinion. When they fail i already know they are weak before entry so i milk them real fast to be positive even if sl hits on final lot. 4. "I talked before about pyramiding your positions as opposed to simply taking your profits." There you will have to go alone buddy. Or convince me they are safe . Actually am pretty happy with my constrainment results and dont want to tweak them. Analytically pyramiding makes sense But i find trading is not just analysis and systems- at the close of a sessions it's psychology that determines pip count. I personally find pyramiding too tough to handle for my nerves. Of course you are free to experiment and post when you get good results. Be sure i would jump at your suggestions. Keep up the good work. Clarification: I am assuming that by pyramiding you mean taking more than twice the normal lot size. I am already taking double of normal lot size. anything more than that will be too much of stress for me.

--- 帖子 #3795 ---
First, some of the trades will be losses and there is nothing you can do about it (this is not a 100% strategy). But in this case, I wouldn't enter as a touch. You can take 35/50 touches only when they are on top of each other and steep. Here they were not only diverging, but they were already start changing direction. Alternatively, you could have waited for a rejecting (green) M5 candle formation on that area and then enter. In this case, there was a full red M5 candle that crossed both M15 35/50, so there was no indication to go long.

Second half of this day is an ugly beast. It’s like a porcupine without the quills. Lots of big bars followed by big bars in the other direction. 1) 10 Touch. The 10 had been steep enough before. Good for 17 to 30 pips, depending on target. 2) 10 Touch. This is the second touch. But MA is steeper now, and there is confluence with Daily R1, RN, and an S/R line. --- 帖子 #3799 ---
Just a quick clarification here duffy. When i say diverging i mean diverging. Actual distance between them might be very small but what i look for is weather this distance is increasing- then i pass it. If they are converging/ parallel / on top then i dont worry about distance much. Of course we are dealing with moving things here and MA always looks better for winners and worse for losers. A winning first touch of 10 EMA will automatically make 10EMA look steep and a losing one will make it look flat. But divergence is not influenced by trade result. In that chart you would notice that i havent marked actual touch as no trade zone but area much before that touch- its not after loss brilliance from me If you do some back testing, i am sure that you will find it saves lots of losing trades. (Actually am much less of a analysis guy and i would rather rely on your expertize there )

bigtent , they dropped because of the news too, the risk appetite decreases, which takes the investors back to the safety of the USD,JPY and CHF. In case of a bad news for the recovery of the global economy or slowing growth of the developing economies the risk appetite falls sharply, and the USD,JPY and CHF rises almost every time in the past 10-12 months. For the Australian dollar it makes a lot of sense, if the Chinese economy slows down, the commodity consumption will drop, and Australia is one of the exporters of iron ore and some others industrial materials, including coal. So if the consumption drops, the exports drops, the economy of Australia slows, and the aussie falls too. It is just played now due to the news

--- 帖子 #3811 ---
OK. This is not a CHOROS rule but I use it very often as an added confirmation in a trade. Somebody may ask why I got in long with that strong short action (even-though the confluence was strong for long)? Answer: I noticed these gaps in the bodies of the M5 bars. In my experience these are getting filled very soon when they form. Even one gap will make me confident about taking a trade in the "filling direction". Here I noticed three in a row! I am not sure why this happens but I tend to believe that these are traps to get most of us in the wrong direction before suddenly reversing in the original direction. So in this case this looked like a bear's trap to me before shooting to the Weekly Pivot... EDIT: As I said, I use these as an added confirmation and not as a signal. My signal was the strong confluence as described in my previous post.

--- 帖子 #3836 ---
Haha, love it! Another example... with the recent floods out here, that flooded some of our biggest coal mines and wiped out a season of crops, they said on the news that the Aussie was going to tumble in a big way, and there was no way it would get back to parity. Then on top of that, we had the biggest cyclone ever in Yasi, wiping out the bulk of the country's sugar cane and banana crops. I forget the figures, but represents a huge dent in our exports and GDP. So what did the Aussie do? Climbed up above parity and is still there, holding fast above US$1.01 for the last week. This makes no sense whatsoever from a funnymental viewpoint. Fact is, the news does NOT drive the markets, trading does, and you can never predict how traders will react to the news, because traders are people and people are not rational nor logical (like to think they are, though). In fact, people are very strange cattle, indeed, and traders, doubly so! This is what attracted me to The Dance (after I saw Kostas equity curve on post 1, of course). The Dance has no "magic or mystery", no "holy grail" system, indicator, etc. As Clay said many times, it relies on the self fulfilling phenomena that traders use moving averages, round numbers, etc, and will react to them, so we want to catch those reactions. In essence, we are trying to judge where and when traders are likely to react and jump on board when they do. The strategy works very well at that. To do this, he found a simple set of Moving Averages that seemed to give the best results. When you realize that nearly all indicators, even oscillators, are a form of moving average, it makes a whole lot of sense in so many ways that the total effect can be summed up in simple set that will expose the likely moves in the market when they agree. Then you "dance around it", reacting rather than predicting. I really admire the genius of that!

--- 帖子 #3874 ---
Yes, because GMT+2 midnight = 5PM EST (US) which is NY close time. Therefore your charts are synchronized to NY close. GMT charts have the "Sunday candle" which is a few hours long. It's actually the Sydney Monday open session and not a "Sunday candle". See the problems we get lining on a big spinning ball in space!?! Bloodywell inconsiderate, I reckon! Anyway... back to the topic..... Pivots are very difficult to use with some brokers for this reason, even those with offset settings to compensate, such as IBFX, who use GMT, but close 1 hour early on Friday (4 pm EST) and open 1 hour later on Monday AEST. Not that you'd want to trade those hours, but it means the last few candles are missing from Friday, and there can be a reasonable movement in that hour, messing up Monday's Pivots! The only way around it would be to have pivots where you could look up the values for the previous close and manually enter them! Another reason I was glad to leave IBFX.

--- 帖子 #3878 ---
Philosophy talk: Great question here. I really hope it doesnt make anyone pessimistic. But very important and intelligent question. Ultimately making or losing money is what matters. In my opinion nothing else matters in trading. Risk reward, success rate, simple or complex - all are BS. real test is - Am i making money. But unfortunately this is wrong question to ask. Because as the manual says, making or losing money is system independent. Your pnl depends on lots of things. System is just one of them. With same system one maybe losing money and another making money. Practical advice: Stop worrying too much about system. No need to get amazing results in back test to apply a system. Even a slight edge is enough. What kills traders is focusing too much on one aspect of trading or looking for holy grail. I would suggest stick with one good system and concentrate on other aspects- psychology, money management etc. My experience: Contrary to what you may believe if you go through my posts, i am not making millions. But reason is not the system. I have mastered only one type of trade and am making lots of money there. But i am tired of waiting for constrainments and get frustrated (psychology) so i am trying to learn touch trades and losing money there. But what this system has done is it has given me enormous confidence. I know i can take pips out of market when i see constrainments. Am getting better at touches and look forward to days when i will master whole of dance. Really pains me that none of old hands are around to post charts or help. Endroute and Kostas are always there but cant ask too much from too few people. Final note: About backtesting- generally results wont be same as live trading. Most of the cases live trading will give much worse result. But once you gain good exp real trading will give much better result . Reasons- you will watch HTF and PA real good. Am sure seniors here don't blindly follow three or four rules. They can see things quite differently than a newbie can.

--- 帖子 #3885 ---
Spot on! Trading is very different to other things. That's why Clay brought up the analogy of "learning to dance", and named the strategy after it. It's also why he said it was NOT a system. You have to learn how to do it, how to feel it, "get in the groove" whatever.... just like dancing. It's not about, if A, do B, etc, like systems in most professions. It's deeper, more intuitive, getting the feel and moving in tune with the market. The charts and rules just help you filter out the market's rhythm, and know when it is out of sych with you so you don't dance (sit out). I was in one of those paid "live trading room" webinar things, and this was one of the things that became obvious. You could NOT learn just by watching and even listening to an experienced trader, because so often discretion and experience comes into it... and how do you explain a "gut feeling"? That's why Clay gave us the Dance Strategy - a framework to work with, AND the simulator, etc, to practice. You have to get the feel, and you can only get that by DOING! It's like learning to ride a bike!

--- 帖子 #3914 ---
Hello everybody I don't know whether this has been discussed before, but in any case here it is: As part of several systems I'm looking into, I've been trying to "quantify" some parameters of the dance as well. I have read the original manual and saw that the idea was creating a system as "mechanical" as possible. I don't know if we are yet to the point where we can build a purely mechanical trading system, but it seems to me that systems like the dance show a great promise for this. Anyway, I was considering -among others- how could we quantify the "trend", the "pullback" and the "MA slope". In order to do this in a generalised way, we have to think in terms of percentage of movement and not pips: Pips are very different from each other, and for example an NZDGBP pip means 3 times more money than an EURUSD pip. So, I see in the manual that a touch on one of the EMAs must have been preceded by a strong pullback/retrace of at least 15 pips. If we assume that those 15 pips were measured in EURUSD, then this would translate roughly to 0.10% movement, and this 0,10% can be applied to all pairs. So if someone is trading the aforementioned NZDGBP, one would consider an acceptable retracement the retracement of 5 pips (= 0,10% for that pair). An area that I think would benefit from quantification, is the steepness of the MA. We can assess that by simply looking at the two last values of the MA. For example, the 10 SMA of the 1H EURUSD chart when the 10:00 GMT candle closed, was 1.3559. 1 hour later, when the 11:00 candle closed, the SMA was 1.3554. So there was a difference of (1.3554-1.3559)*100/1.3554 = -0.037%. As we see that the 10 SMA in the 1H chart is pretty steep, and by looking at different SMAs and making a few calculations, we can perhaps say that for a Moving Average to be deemed "steep", the difference between the last two SMA values must be over 0.15-0.20% (absolute value). This way we can have a measurable criterion for deciding whether an MA is steep enough for a trade to be taken, which could be useful if we also think that the "steepness" is in the eye of the beholder and can be influenced by the way each of us has set up his or her charts. I have other ideas for identifying and quantifying a "trend", a "constrainment" etc, so that perhaps we can move towards an even more mechanical system which would reduce the discretionary decisions to simple speculations on how the price would react on round numbers, support/resistance levels, pivot points or news releases. If the above makes any sense to any of you, let me know

Here's something else I just learned about and could be quite helpful; Price tends to fill the voids. ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++ You are 100% correct. What the rules for the trend line we're trying to implement here, are not yet written. Basically (in my mind) there are 2 flavors of trendlines. The most common of which I call the "Common Sense Trend Line". This trend line uses tops or bottoms &amp; sometimes both, to connect the dots. The second is the "Tom DeMark Trend Line". This has it's own precise way to drawn. The 1st pic below shows a valid swing point. In this case a high candle followed &amp; preceded by 2 candles with lower highs. The opposite for swing lows. A valid Tom DeMark trend line (2nd pic) uses only the most recent 2 swing points. The Tom DeMark trend line also has a price projection based on the highest price above the trend line (second pic) and a vertical line from it, which intersects the trend line below. In this case you would subtract the total number of pips from this calc, from the point at which price intersects and remains below the trend line. I've completed extensive back testing on this price projection and found it to work quite well on 15m to 4hr trend lines. 5m is just not reliable enough. The best results over 68 set ups was in the eur/jpy. 3827 pips profit vs. 464 loss. The rub here is that this test covered several months, 24/7. Somehow I need to sleep so the story makes a good movie but the book is too lengthy. Sorry to get so far off topic. My thoughts are if we're gonna use trend lines, the more resources we have the better we can use them.

--- 帖子 #3946 ---
G'day folks, Attached is the MA to help deal with the bending snakes tongue of the 10 EMA. I don't think there is any need to fiddle with the 35 and 50 as the tongue-wagging is insignificant. Basically this MA has varying thickness to show when the MA is "steep enough" as well as some lines at the front that do NOT move, unlike the serpent's tongue. We have all seen the cases where the price is nowhere near the snake's tongue when price hits the low of the candle, but when it comes back up and finishes, the MA is touching the candle. So this is an attempt to help us catch these. The idea is having some static lines, that do NOT move, that we can use along with price action to guesstimate where an eventual touch will be. It's like trying to define a "possible touch zone". You can turn them on or off, and change the colours and styles of each. Maybe this will help maybe it won't, but they're there for you to test out! In summary, this MA has: varying line thickness (or style) to show the real slope of the line (regardless of chart scale). This is achieved by setting " Trend_Minimum " to a pip value (I use 1.5 for the M15 10 EMA), and if the MA moves more than the set pips per bar, then it is highlighted. Note that you will need other values for different time frames. To set the highlight colours and styles, you need to to go to the settings tab. The first four buffer settings should be the same (they are the highlighted setting) and the last two are for when the MA is "too flat". These are my settings (the colour is the same but the line thickens when it is at a valid slope)..... Attached Image Attached Image (click to enlarge) Show_last_true basically draws a horizontal line at the level the MA was at the close of the last candle. This is the last "true" value since the MA is an average of the close and this is the last candle to actually close. Show_MA_at_open This shows where the moving average was at the opening of the current candle. If the current candle ends up closing as a doji, this is where the MA will end up! Show_Projection_1 and Show_Projection_2 are basically the same as each other. They project a line forward equal to the slope of the average over the last few bars. They have variable start positions (1 = the last candle, 2 = 2 candles back, etc), and the length determines how many candles to measure the slope over. Defaults for Projection_1 are: start at 1 and length of 1, which means it uses the slope of the MA between the last candle and the one before it. Defaults for Projection_2 are: start at 1 and length of 5, so this uses the average slope of the MA for last 5 candles. Project_forward draws the lines a little longer (1 bar "into the future") so that when the price comes down the line is either side of the candle, making it a little easier to see when it crosses, etc Hope it helps! Attached File(s) MA extended-2.mq4 22 KB | 378 downloads

Yes, it's there. It "snapshots" the spread when it initializes and then at the beginning of each bar. This is because the spread keeps changing and trailing stops which use the current value of spread end up constantly updating the stop, so you have to have a more constant value. --- 帖子 #4005 ---
Using my scripts, I have the risk set to 2% per trade, at a standard stop of 15 pips (I don't add spread), and two trades, which means each is a 1% risk. My script uses strict risk, meaning that it will open the trade at a lot size that will be less than or equal to the set risk. Last week I funded my GoMarkets minilot account with a very small amount. It was so small that, opening 2 trades, I was not able to open trades at my full risk amount, as each part of the trade was at the minimum lot size, and if it were incremented 1 step, it would exceed the 2% limit. So the total risk I ended up with was just over 1%. That meant I had to work a bit harder to build the account. Which is good in 2 ways, it reduces the risk at the beginning and making it a little tougher to gain is good for my development. Tonight I got my balance to a level which means my next trade will be actually at the 2%, and my next trade will be double the lot size of my last, so compounding has actually started. Of course, 1 loss, and it's automatically back to the lower risk. For me, that is a minor milestone reached! Yes it is only "early days", but the stats on that were only 4 positions (2 trades) losers out of 18 positions (9 trades) and only 1 of the losers was a full loss. My rationale on the very small real money account is that it is not a significant risk personally, but it is real money and as I become successful, it will grow into a realistic account, and I will grow with it psychologically, and be able to trade it. I highly recommend people to consider this when starting out, as, to me, that makes much more sense than spending time on demo, and then having to swap to a real account, and deal with the psychological step as well as forego profits while learning. Maybe it is beginners luck, but I have been trying to trade 4x for almost 3 years and have paid for courses and "live trading rooms", but never seen anything that works like this style of trading, and I have never seen so many people getting consistent results like Kostas and others, and it has been the Dance/CHOROS that has turned them around. Every day I am learning to read the market in ways that I never could before with all the other systems, paid and unpaid. I have a long way to go to make back all that I lost over that period, but I truly believe that I can do it. Once again, thanks to Clay, Kostas, Survivor, Duffypratt, and all the other contributors to this thread and the original Dance thread.

--- 帖子 #4017 ---
I've been trying to compile a "checklist", something to take a look at before each trade and perhaps evaluate the chance of a successful entry. I have tried to make it rather general to fit most situations. What would you add/remove/change in the list below ? 1) Is the (Pip Value * Spread) of the pair acceptable ? 2) Is the pair trending well ? (parallel moving averages of good slope - no "porcupine") 3) Is the trade in the direction of the trend as defined by your preferred moving averages ? 4) Is the price on the trendy side of the moving averages ? 5) If entering on a pullback, is the pullback sufficiently big ? 6) Is the trade supported by a valid touch on a moving average in 5M/15M/1H/4H/1D ? 6a) If yes, is the MA acceptably steep ? 6b) If yes, has the touch occured sufficiently quickly (eg in 1 or 2 candles) ? 7) Is the trade supported by a valid price level ? (valid = not having been breached more than 1-3 times in the vicinity of the timeframe) 7a) Round Number ? 7b) Previous Day or Week High/Low ? 7c) Daily/Weekly/Monthly pivot point (Pivot/S1/S2/R1/R2) ? 7d) Fibonacci retracement ? 7e) Some other S/R not falling in the above categories ? 8) Is there price constrainment in any of the above lines ? 9) Is the trade supported by a characteristic candle pattern in 5M/15M/1H/4H/1D ? (pinbars, IB, OB, double tops/bottoms, etc) ? 10) Is the trade supported by the setup of relevant currency pairs (eg reversal indications in both EURUSD and GBPUSD) ?

--- 帖子 #4021 ---
I think that we have to realize some of the inherent "nuances" of 4x. If there was a central market, then there would be one price and it would be a "correct" price, but forex has no central market. It is a distributed market, made up of thousands of banks and brokers who's computers communicate between themselves through various routes and clusters and somehow arbitrate a price. It's like a horde of hagglers all hollering at once, and it's amazing that it functions as well as it does. That communication is NOT instantaneous, and, because of this, there is no "correct price" as such, and you will always get variations, especially when there is fast action during news. That is also a reason for the spread variation during news... it's not all "broker manipulation", as some think (but brokers can take advantage of that and add to the confusion).

Most systems, you find out when the market is not right for your system (trend, range, whatever) only AFTER a few failed trades (ouch!). With the Dance, you can pretty much see when it is likely to get choppy or turn or range, and you can stay out, with caution, etc. It doesn't predict the future, but it does help avoid the nasties! --- 帖子 #4049 ---
The spread jumps so much because Oanda is a market maker and has to protect itself in those times. If you think you want to trade the news, you should consider looking at an ECN or an STP. I'm using MBTrading. The spreads definitely go up, but I have not yet seen spreads as big as you are reporting. Then, at the end of one of those big news runs, the reverse happens, and sometimes the spreads actually go negative for short periods of times. The difference is that an ECN makes money off commission on trades. They pass through the best bid and ask from the different bank feeds that they use and (also from their own internal customers). Those will get crazy during news times, but what you see and pay is closer to the real thing. The risk here, of course, is that there may be slippage or re-quotes. With a market maker like Oanda, you will likely get a quicker fill, but that's because Oanda has already protected itself from really large moves by boosting the spread. Oanda has at that time guaranteed your fill and taken a position against you. It will then try to pass on your trade either to another of it's customers or to the interbank. Thus, for the brief time that it's holding your position, its trading against you and will continue to be against you until it can balance its own risk. Either way, entering trades during news is risky. With an ECN, you face higher spreads and the possibility of some slippage. With a market maker, you face much higher spreads, less slippage, but the possibility that the broker takes some action against your interest because they are on the opposite side of the trade from you.

EO's manual talks about a rather complicated set of MAs: 15M chart: 5 ema, 10 ema, 21 ema, 35 sma, 50 ema, 200 sma 1H chart: 10 sma, 50 sma, 62 ema, 200 sma 4H chart: 5 sma, 10 sma, 50 ema, 150 ema 1D chart: 5 sma, 35 sma, 50 ema Don't ask me why eg the 50 is usually an EMA but in 1H charts it's an SMA. Best justification I've seen about the choice of some MA is that "it's what the big boys use". But actually I think it can't be proved that price respects more the 50 EMA than the 43 SMA or the 57 WMA. Probably they will all experience the same number of bounces. I think they serve mostly as a reminder that price has moved too much in one direction and the probability of a reversal increases.

I wrote my chart up before I saw this. Here are my comments on what you have here. 1-3 are before London opening, and thus not strictly dance. On 3, the rule that the pullback to the 35 or 50 must be two bars is new. It's not in the original dance rules, or in the original thread, and lots of people do not observe it. I've read the rules in the latest manual a few times, and I'm not entirely certain that Clay means it. I think this is an OK, but not a great trade. 6 and 7 are bounces off the M5. Clay includes the M5 as one of the MAs in the first manual, but I don't think he actually recommended using it. (I could be wrong on this.) I think some others here don't even put it on their charts. Recently, there seems to be more interest in using it to get in on really quick, big moves. I'm interested in the idea, but I haven't really started looking for these touches yet. 8-11 These would all be counter-trend entries. You raise an interesting question here. Dance says go with the trend of the moment, which is defined by price in relation to the 35/50. But is it possible that there is a steep enough move, even with price on the other side, so that you would go against the Dance defined trend? I'm not sure about this. If there is, I would think it has to qualify as an "advanced" technique. What you have generally looks good to me. And you have an economy with words that I regrettably lack. If you put up a chart like this in the future, I'll chime in with comments, and do my own analysis on another pair. That's fine with me. In my opinion, the more charts, the better.

Thanks for pointing out those posts. I think the "2 bar rule" for 35/50 trades must be an area where Clay used his judgment, but formulated a "rule" for beginners. Take a look at this post: http://www.forexfactory.com/showthre...=224697&amp;page=4 There are three possible trades here. The first one definitely violates the two bar rule, but it's still a good trade according to Clay. It takes four bars for price to make a "near touch" on the 35. Also interesting here is the idea of taking this trade on the "clear break" of the 10 as confirmation. The second possible trade here Clay dismisses, because it took too long for price to get to the 35. We would now say that that's a two bar violation, but here Clay is using a judgment call, instead of invoking a rule. Then on the third trade, there is a strong two bar move down to the 50, and Clay says this is the best trade. But even here, its not exactly clear to me how you would count bars using a rule. All those bars that led up to trade 2, which was no good, also led up to trade 3. There is a slight upswing before price comes down again, but I don't think the little upswing counts as a "reset" according to some rule. Again, I think this is an area for judgment, as opposed to the strict application of rules. (Take a look to the left on the third trade and you will see that, in addition to the strong move to the 50, there is really good support and resistance at this level as well). However, if you project slope of the 10 from the earlier bars, this would have been a touch by about .4 pips. The subsequent action makes it look like a no touch, when in real time its a perfectly good trade (or at least a decent judgment call). What this means is that back testing has a tendency to show winning trades that traders would miss in real time, and to make things look like obvious losers when they would have been OK trades in real time. All that aside, I think this is a perfectly valid, by the rules touch trade. If you took it at the projected touch on this bar, it's good for 10 to up to 15 pips (15 if you took it perfectly and set TP for 15). There was some discussion of waiting for confirmation last night. I think waiting for confirmation makes lots of sense for bounce trades, or when there are lots of support layers underneath a trade and you don't know where the bounce will actually come. --- 帖子 #4119 ---
I have realized that often I trail my stops too aggressively and this can result to losses. And I mean overall losses, not just on a specific trade. If we use a take profit level that is equal to our stop loss and enter the market at a random moment, there would be on average 50% chances for our take profit to be hit before our stop loss. This means that in the long run we would only lose the spread, even with totally random entries. A refined entry by the Dance rules (or any other working system) needs only improve our chances so much as to overcome the spread in order to be profitable in the long run. But if we move our stop loss to BE+1 very soon or if we take profits that are less than our risk too often (as I have been guilty of doing), then we need EXTREMELY good entries in order to be profitable. I used to think that if I can secure a few pips then that's a good thing because I won't lose the trade, but if those pips are too few then I'm just compromising my trade's chance to provide me as much reward as my risk. Think about this: We enter long at 1.3500 with a stop loss of 20 pips (at 1.3480) and a take profit of 20 pips (at 1.3520). We see price going up to 1.3507, returning down to 1.3490 etc. We feel anxious that perhaps we did not have a good entry, so as soon as price climbs to 1.3515, we move our stop loss to 1.3510. We are happy because we have secured 10 pips and our trade is still running. But now the price has 50% chances of going up to our target of 1.3520 and 50% chances of hitting our stop loss of 1.3510. So after many such trades, the average profit will be 15 pips (half of the time price will climb to 1.3520 for a 20-pip profit and the other half it will go down to 1.3510 for a 10-pip profit). Meanwhile, when price doesn't go our way, we will usually suffer the whole 20 pips of loss waiting for it to hit our stop loss. While we will move our stop loss to 1.3510 when price climbs to 1.3515, we will not accordingly readjust our take profit to 1.3490 (or simply close the trade) when price goes to 1.3485... So the result of many such trades will be a net loss of (2.5 pips + spread) per trade. We need better than random entries just to offset that loss . We need MUCH better than random entries in order to be profitable. So in the above scenario of the random entry, we should move up our stop loss only to a level that is ABOVE our take profit. Or, just grab our profit when it is as much as our risk. Then, with a good entry system, we can overcome the spread and become profitable. Now I have to practice what I preach

--- 帖子 #4120 ---
I agree with your conclusion, but not with your reasoning. Assuming a perfect random walk, moving to BE at any pre-defined point will make no difference. Let's say we are talking a game of flipping a coin. Your take profit will occur when you get 20 more heads than tails. Your stop loss is when you get 20 more tails than heads. But, when you get plus 15 heads, you will move your stop to plus 10 heads. In the coin game, what difference does this make in the long run? The answer is: none at all. Expectancy is still zero. There is no money management decision you can make in a coin game that will increase your expectancy over the long run. If there were, then some type of Martingale system would be able to beat a casino. Fortunately, when it comes to markets, the random walk and efficient market theories are bunk. I didn't say why I agreed with the conclusion. Basically, good traders seem all to agree that it's best to cut losers short and to let winners run. There are lot's of good reasons for that idea. The whole idea of trending and momentum agrees with that. I know of some people who claim that random entries, combined with a good exit strategy can lead to profits. From what I've seen, those exit strategies tend to look for some home-runs and quite a few strikeouts. From all the testing I've done, and from everything I've read, smaller stops and larger TPs generally lead to bigger profits. But there are two catches to this approach: First is psychology. It's just as true that losing tends to lead to bad decisionmaking, which in turn leads to more losing. That's the biggest reason why moving to BE is a good idea. It can help prevent the losing spiral and self-destruction. The other catch is capital preservation. If you adopt a strategy that wins say 1/3rd of the time, and can have 8-10 losses in a row on a fairly regular basis, you may end up with really significant problems with drawdown. Remember, that a 50% gain and a 50% loss are the same in dollar amounts, but you need to make a 100% profit to recoup a 50% loss, while you only need to lose 33% to blow a 50% gain. That's another reason why locking in gains can be so important, even if its not the best theoretical money-maker.

--- 帖子 #4123 ---
Your coin example is not analogous; when you have 15 heads in a row you can't go back to 10 heads in a row. I'll try to make myself clear this way: Let's pretend for a moment that spread doesn't exist. Let's also pretend that one makes totally random entries in the one hour chart and sets a take profit of 50 pips and a stop loss of 50 pips. Do we agree that without a spread, this is a zero-sum game in the long run ? Ok, now suppose that this person, EVERY TIME that the prices goes 25 pips his way, moves his stop loss ONE pip behind price and keeps trailing his stop by ONE pip. How many times do you think he will reach the take profit of 50 pips ? Very rarely. His wins will almost always be less than 50 pips. But his losses will always be 50 pips. The result will be great losses for him. So you can't make a decision that will make you profitable in the long run when your entry is random. But you can certainly make decisions that will make you lose.

--- 帖子 #4124 ---
If you were right, and that sort of system would generate losses, then doing exactly the opposite would be a winning system. When the expectancy is 0, and the events are truly random, like with the coin flip, there is no way to concoct either a winning or a losing strategy. Also, about my analogy. I wasn't talking about 10 winners in a row. The bet is this: I win if we reach a point where there have been 20 more heads than tails. I lose if we get 20 more tails than heads. So, if the first toss is heads and the next is tails, the net is 0. The game continues until we are at plus or minus 20. But, I also have decided to move my losing point to +10 when I hit the point where there are 15 more heads than tails. I think this is the point you are missing: If you move the stop loss, of course your average profits on winning trades will be less. And of course, your average loss on losing trades will stay the same. But the winning percentage will go up at the same time. If there's really no edge one way or another because its all random, then where you put the stops, the break even points, and the take profits, will make no difference at all over the long run. As I said before, there is no money management system that will increase or decrease a casinos edge over time. It simply is what it is, no matter how the bettor tries to scale his bets. The big difference between casinos and markets is that markets simply are not totally random. And to the extent that they are random, it's in a very different way from the randomness of casinos. In a casino, the number 22 coming up on a roulette wheel 25 times in a row is astronomically small. In a market, that kind of freak even happens pretty regularly. As an example, volatility in equities destroyed Long Term Capital Management back in 1998. According to the math models, using gaussian distributions, the volatility that they experienced at that time was a 10 sigma event. That means that its the sort of thing that one would expect to see maybe once in several times the life of the universe. (The 1987 market crash was another such event. So was the mini crash that lasted a few hours earlier this year.) OK, so it happened once and that doesn't necessarily prove the model wrong. But, again in 1999 the markets saw an even greater increase in equity volatility.

--- 帖子 #4125 ---
Interesting conversation. Remember that Clay dismissed these probability based tenets completely and there is good reason to do so. The "coin toss" entry is not valid in markets for the following reason. The coin toss is a 50/50 because it is based on only two possible outcomes - right/wrong, or win/lose, whereas the market can and usually does move up and down by varying amounts, which is why they say it "winds" up or down. So you have to introduce another variable..... "how far?". As soon as another variable is introduced, the 50/50 has flown out the window! Also, you cannot go validly go all hypothetical, and pretend the spread is not there, etc, because once you do, you are no longer talking about the markets, and any conclusions drawn cannot be applied to the real markets. The spread is always there, and therefore price will always have to move that extra amount for a TP to occur, than it would for a stop, so it cannot ever be 50/50. Statistics and the application of probablity can be useful in many applications, bu they can also be very misleading. For example, an average 25 degrees C is a nice comfortably warm temperature. So therefore, if your feet are in dry ice at about -60 and your head is being steamed at 110, the average is 25, so you'd be quite comfortable, correct? A trading example of the application of "probability", and this does occur...... People are trading a system that has a long standing track record of 60% winning trades. So they deduce that is the probability of the system, and that over time in the future, they will achieve that by religiously trading the system. They will even go further, and say that a string of losses, means that a good run of wins is just around the corner, because it will have to do this to bring the percentage back to 60%. Complete and utter bollocks! Past performance statistics are exactly that and not "probability" at all, and there is no validity in assuming that it will continue in the future. Probability can only determined if all the possibilities can be defined or behaviour will continue in the same way it has previously, and in trading, they cannot and it may not. If they could do this, the Holy Grail EA would be very simple indeed, and we could all kick our heels up and watch the $$$ roll in! Also, Kostas more often than not takes profits smaller than his stop, and if he splits the trade, he usually only allows a very small part of it run, cashing in on the majority of the trade. So why are we all on this thread, trying to emulate Kostas' success? According to the assumptions above, that is poor Risk/Reward ratio handling and therefore he must be a loser! Clay is very aggressive with his stops, and trails aggressively. The SBE+1 is an example of this. The main thing about the Dance is learning to read the market, using the MA's and rules to help do this, and take what is on the table when you can. It is not a system, but a strategy that helps you develop the discretion needed to become profit. In many ways that is more art than science and it is why Clay said that statistics and risk/reward ratios, etc, were counterproductive. We do not need to hit the ball out of the park. We need to make profitable trades, and that is about reading the market to time your entries, and also your exits. "Cut your losses and let your profits run" is often touted. Well, cut your losses for sure, but we are traders, not investors, so taking what is on the table is far better than waiting for some arbitrary price that achieve your risk/reward ratio and having the market turn and take you out! The market is not something that rewards "bravery" or daring, and any open trade is at risk and even more so the longer it remains open! Don't forget the other idiom - "No one ever went broke by taking profits".

Great discussion. I think Survivor has nailed many of the reasons for people leaving the forums. The only thing I will add is the sheer repetitive nature of some of the discussion. I can't speak for EOHater, but it's possible that he thought that after 1000 pages, he just didn't want to repeat himself anymore, and that there should be enough on the forum for people to get it. As for the question about why Clay's mentor would start small accounts again and again, and then grow them quickly. I can think of several reasons. First, he might have done it simply because he could. Second, it's possible he did that while he was teaching other people, and that he was also trading larger accounts, maybe as a swing trader, at the same time. Third, he might have done it as a way of testing new ideas, or new wrinkles to his methods. Fourth, he might simply have done it for the challenge. Finally, it might have been an integral part of his money management system. He makes a certain amount of money from a small account, and then pulls it out of the market and puts it into safer investments, or uses it to fund his lifestyle, or whatever. Rinse and repeat. And it's possible that he learned that after he hit a million, his fear and greed took over. Lots and lots of reasons why it might happen, and they could work in combination. I totally agree with the observation about leaving only a small amount of money at any broker. That's the real irony of the new leverage regulations. Let's say I got really successful and had a million dollars to trade with. And lets also say that I was willing to risk 2%/trade (or $20,000). If brokers offered 100:1 leverage, I would put $100-150K in the brokerage account, and put the rest of the money into fairly liquid investments, so that my passive money could work for me. If I hit a bad run, I might get a margin call and then refund the account, but I would only have a small amount of my money doing nothing in a risky (bankruptcy/dishonesty) brokerage account. The reduction to 50:1 leverage means doubling the amount needed in the brokerage account, and reducing the amount that could otherwise be working for me. (This is purely theoretical at this point, but one can hope and plan.) On top of that, I personally believe that gains made in a brokerage account aren't fully "real" until they have been withdrawn and are available for use at something other than trading. Once I hit a certain level, I plan to start withdrawing money regularly. This might not be the best for the trading account, but if I get there, I'm sure it will do wonders for the psychological aspect. I have a friend nearby who has been trading for at least 8 years. He's the one who finally convinced me to get interested. He pretty much started with nothing (maybe $500 or $1000). At least three times, he has grown his account to over a million. One of those times, I think he was in the multi-million range. He's very aggressive as a trader, and each time, he got overconfident and came close to losing everything. Now, he's taking money out of his account as he makes it, growing more slowly, and it looks like its finally working as a long term thing for him. There was never any problem with his basic methods. The losses all came from failure to follow his own rules, and from doubting his systems too early (before his plan called for doubts). Now he seems to have found a money management program that fits both with his personality and his trading.
